Wichita

Wichita is a broader people-level reading route, while Wichita and Affiliated Tribes is the name of a present government centered at Anadarko, Oklahoma. Its institutional history includes Wichita Proper, Waco, Taovaya, Tawakoni and Kichai, whose names and histories should remain individually identified. This community-source foundation follows the Tribe’s account of Plains village life, displacement, continuing community and educational resources; it does not make the historical labels interchangeable or establish every present affiliation.

Start reading here

Wichita is a broader historical and people-level route linked to Wichita and Affiliated Tribes; Waco, Tawakoni, Taovaya and Kichai labels are not interchangeable. The four exhibit chapters count as one work. Newsletter history is retrospective, while the 2024 paper's selected methods and discussion do not include its detailed results, maps or underlying interviews.

  1. Wichita Memories — four connected institutional history chapters

    The Tribe's connected Wichita Memories chapters provide an introductory historical narrative with the cooperative exhibit's authorship and scope visible.

  2. Removal from Texas — Wichita History, August 2012 newsletter, pp. 2–3

    This Tribal newsletter article distinguishes Waco and Tawakoni removal from the Wichita and Keechi journey instead of flattening them into one route.

  3. English to Wichita — official dictionary listing

    The official dictionary offers a concrete route into Wichita vocabulary and short phrases; its audio and apps were not tested.

  4. Anchoring Sovereignty in Space: Documenting Places of Wichita Community Building in the Twentieth Century — selected sections

    Selected collaborative-research sections connect twentieth-century community gathering places with archaeological methods and attributed memories.

These are selected starting points. The full annotated collection, source perspectives, inspection limits and remaining research questions follow below. A starting guide is not an exhaustive history or community endorsement.

01

Named peoples and a present government

The Tribe’s history identifies Wichita Proper, Waco, Taovaya, Tawakoni and Kichai within its account. Its later chapter describes the organized Wichita and Affiliated Tribes community at Anadarko. Keep those two levels clear: related historical peoples are not simply alternate spellings, and this institutional account does not make every historical group one timeless government. Other historical and community sources should be read with their dates and named scope. The dated Elam and Harper accounts also distinguish narrower and broader uses of Wichita; their historical terminology must be read in context.

Read the sources [1] Wichita and Affiliated Tribes; exhibit collaboration credited to the Stovall Museum of Science and History and Oklahoma Archaeological Survey [2] Wichita and Affiliated Tribes [6] Wichita and Affiliated Tribes [9] Texas State Historical Association, Handbook of Texas Online [7] Oklahoma Historical Society, The Chronicles of Oklahoma; digitization at The Gateway to Oklahoma History / UNT Libraries

02

Farming, hunting and the seasonal village

The People of the Grass House chapter describes a seasonal pattern combining gardens and buffalo hunting. It follows food preservation and storage alongside the work of maintaining grass houses. Read this as a historical account of particular Plains village practices, including cooperative household work, rather than a picture of how every Wichita person lives today. Cultural and ceremonial narratives in the original remain with their publisher.

Read the sources [1] Wichita and Affiliated Tribes; exhibit collaboration credited to the Stovall Museum of Science and History and Oklahoma Archaeological Survey

03

Red River trade and changing villages

Harper places Taovaya settlements on both sides of the Red River and discusses related villages sharing trade centers. Her interpretation supports historical Texas connections while retaining separate names; it does not establish a fixed territory. The underlying colonial records remain unread here.

Read the sources [7] Oklahoma Historical Society, The Chronicles of Oklahoma; digitization at The Gateway to Oklahoma History / UNT Libraries

04

Reading the 1846 Council Springs treaty

The May 15, 1846 treaty names Wichita, Waco and other participating groups separately. Its text addresses trade, prisoners, violence, peace, and proposed blacksmith and teaching services. The printed signatory list also retains distinct period headings. Readers can examine a primary agreement here while keeping its limits clear: stated promises are not proof of implementation, and historical names or signatures alone do not settle present identity, jurisdiction or treaty rights.

Read the sources [11] Oklahoma State University Libraries, Tribal Treaties Database; Indian Affairs: Laws and Treaties

05

Texas displacement and wartime refuge

The Tribe’s August 2012 history distinguishes Waco and Tawakoni removal from the Brazos Reserve from the Wichita and Keechi journey through the Fort Arbuckle area. Neighbors’s September 3, 1859 report, reprinted in 1883, dates his Texas-reserve party’s arrival to August 16 and the administrative handover to September 1. He also reports that people were unwilling to occupy new homes without protection. Those official dates do not establish safety, voluntary migration or one identical journey for every named people. Individual registers and fuller route records remain unreviewed. The Tribe’s account later describes wartime flight to Kansas and a return to Indian Territory.

Read the sources [10] Wichita and Affiliated Tribes [1] Wichita and Affiliated Tribes; exhibit collaboration credited to the Stovall Museum of Science and History and Oklahoma Archaeological Survey [14] United States Senate / Government Printing Office; GovInfo digital copy

06

A later petition and the limits of official records

The collection also prints an April 1882 petition by delegates identifying Wichita, Caddo and “Pannatakees,” using that period wording. They ask Congress to confirm land held in common. This preserves their stated claim, not a finding that the claim was accepted or proof of every community’s position. Keeping the petition separate from officials’ interpretations helps readers compare whose account each record presents.

Read the sources [14] United States Senate / Government Printing Office; GovInfo digital copy

07

Continuity through family and community

A New Beginning emphasizes continuing community after the loss of grass-house village life. The account describes older and younger generations sharing memories while people pursue education, employment and family gatherings. Its language of endurance is the institution’s interpretation of its history; it is not a statistical survey or a claim that every member has the same experience or practice.

Read the sources [1] Wichita and Affiliated Tribes; exhibit collaboration credited to the Stovall Museum of Science and History and Oklahoma Archaeological Survey

08

Community memory beyond a story of disappearance

Bethke, Trabert and Gary McAdams’s collaborative research with Wichita and Affiliated Tribes brings community memories together with archives and low-impact archaeology. The authors describe how twentieth-century gathering places in Oklahoma helped sustain relationships through and after allotment. Their account connects older history with living Wichita people. It remains a specific community-based study: its published recollections and academic interpretation should be attributed, rather than treated as a survey of every community or a current legal boundary.

Read the sources [8] American Antiquity / Society for American Archaeology; Cambridge University Press

09

A public route into the language

The Tribe’s online dictionary pairs English vocabulary and phrases with Wichita forms and links many entries for pronunciation. Readers can follow this community-published resource directly. The listing was inspected, but recordings and apps were not tested. Resource availability alone does not establish current speaker totals, proficiency or learning outcomes.

Read the sources [4] Wichita and Affiliated Tribes

10

Language learning and community-controlled archives

Sapphire Hodges’s 2018 thesis examines archives and language-learning possibilities in a Wichita community setting. Her account describes Tribal direction of an archive project and argues for community control over learning priorities. The survey was largely voluntary at a local event, included people with different community relationships, and used self-assessed language ability. It is a dated case study, not a census or a test of present proficiency. The Tribe’s Department of Preservation separately describes its History Center, archives, library and language projects; listing a resource does not make all its materials public or establish learning outcomes.

Read the sources [12] University of Oklahoma, MA thesis in Applied Linguistic Anthropology; SHAREOK institutional repository [13] Wichita and Affiliated Tribes

11

Education as a contemporary institution

The Education Services Department describes support ranging from adult and vocational learning to undergraduate and graduate study. Its program account also discusses lending equipment for coursework. These are the publisher’s stated activities and aims. Funding, eligibility and application requirements vary; this guide does not promise assistance or report measured outcomes. The original pages remain the route to current details.

Read the sources [5] Wichita and Affiliated Tribes, Education Services Department

12

Reading path and the scope of this foundation

Begin with the Tribe’s connected history exhibit, then compare its more specific newsletter account of removal with the 1846 treaty text and the later federal compilation of the 1859 report and 1882 petition. Use the public dictionary and education pages as direct community-published routes. Harper’s trade-history pages, the collaborative twentieth-century study and Hodges’s language/archive case study ask different questions and should retain their dates, methods and perspectives. Further primary records, separately scoped affiliated histories and governing-text review remain open. This is a developing cited source guide, not a completed or community-endorsed history.

Wichita Memories — four connected institutional history chapters ↗

Four linked chapters explain the Tribe’s historical account from early encounters through village life, displacement and continuing community. The credits identify a cooperative exhibit. Treat the chapters as one work, keep named historical groups distinct, and attribute archaeological, treaty and continuity interpretations rather than turning the narrative into independently checked archival evidence.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Complete main narratives of In the Beginning:1540–1750 (lines27–38), People of the Grass House:1750–1820 (27–39), Days of Darkness:1820–1934 (27–37), and A New Beginning:1934–Present (27–38), plus References and Contributors (27–91). Public narrative passages read; no quoted origin stories, ceremonial details, images or underlying bibliography reproduced or separately researched.

Review recorded: October 26, 2026

Access note: Public readable English HTML, no account/paywall encountered. Individual publication/revision dates are unstated; date ranges in titles are historical coverage, not publication dates. Do not repeat historical population estimates as current figures, infer present identities from archaeological phases, or treat institutional treaty summaries as direct readings of the instruments.

Inspected material and access routes

Community-Based Archives, Museums and Language Revitalization: A Case Study from the Wichita and Affiliated Tribes in Anadarko, Oklahoma — selected sections ↗

Hodges, Sapphire. 2018. Community-Based Archives, Museums and Language Revitalization: A Case Study from the Wichita and Affiliated Tribes in Anadarko, Oklahoma. MA thesis, University of Oklahoma. https://hdl.handle.net/11244/299837.

Publication: 2018

Selected chapters connect community-controlled archives with language-learning possibilities. Methods and participation limits are explicit: surveys were largely collected at a community event, and responses are not a population census or proficiency assessment. Read the author’s recommendations as a dated interpretation, not proof of present outcomes.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Actual PDF text: title/degree/copyright/contents/abstract; introduction pp. 1–3; Sections 3.3–3.4 pp. 84–90 plus opening self-assessment caveat in 3.5 p. 90; Section 4.1 pp. 130–134; Chapter 6 “Final Thoughts,” pp. 180–186. Printed page number = PDF zero-based page index minus 7. Surrounding returned excerpts were encountered, but detailed survey-result sections, grammar appendix, underlying archive materials and recordings were not systematically inspected or reproduced.

Review recorded: October 26, 2026

Access status: Public searchable English PDF and repository metadata, no account required

Access note: 247 PDF pages were available; only the specified sections are reviewed. The author reports mostly voluntary participation at the Annual Dance, mixed participant relationships/enrollment, and self-assessed language ability without a standardized proficiency instrument. Do not extrapolate this convenience sample to all citizens or treat an academic category as a citizenship determination. The study’s archive account partly rests on an interview with a project consultant; the underlying interview was not inspected. The 2018 dates and tentative recommendations must remain visible. No present fluent-speaker count, guaranteed revitalization outcome or community endorsement is claimed.

Land in the Indian Territory — selected 1859 removal report and 1882 delegates’ petition ↗

United States Senate. Land in the Indian Territory. Senate Executive Document 13, 48th Congress, 1st session, ordered printed December 19, 1883. Selected report of Robert S. Neighbors, September 3, 1859, p. 26; petition of delegates, April 1, 1882, p. 28.

Publication: 1883

This federal collection preserves an official removal account beside an Indigenous delegates’ petition. Their different dates, authors and purposes matter: arrival and administrative handover are not proof of consent, and a petition records a stated claim rather than a legal determination.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Actual 84-page public PDF: cover/front matter p. 1; complete Robert S. Neighbors report dated September 3, 1859, printed/PDF p. 26; complete delegates’ petition dated April 1, 1882, p. 28, ending at its date/attestation before a separate Cheyenne–Arapaho text. Nearby estimates and later official arguments were encountered for context, not adopted as findings.

Review recorded: October 27, 2026

Access status: Public English scanned PDF with extractable OCR; normal direct download succeeded

Access note: Web tool rejected the 57,166,188-byte file as too large; normal HTTP 200 retrieval succeeded. No manuscript comparison or independent verification of the agent’s satisfaction/property claims. The letter does not independently identify every people in the Tribe’s later removal narrative. Petition boundaries, historic labels and claims are not converted into present territories, identities or legal rights.
